@@18716997 <p> If you think " urban heat islands " sound like a rather pleasant tropical cityscape destination , you would be wrong . They are highly populated metropolitan areas that are heating faster than their rural surroundings due to human activity , and according to a new assessment , this is going to cost them -- both environmentally and economically -- dearly . <p> A new study on the impact of climate change on cities suggests 25 percent of the world 's cities could be 7 ? C warmer by the end of the century , and they face paying twice the economic cost to fight climate change than the rest of the world . The study is published in Nature Climate Change . <p> Cities heat up faster than other areas because of the concentrated energy released from traffic , building insulation , and industrial output combined with heat being trapped by large cities ' dark concrete buildings , asphalt roads , and close together structures . <p> The international team of economists analyzed the policies of 1,692 cities in the hopes of helping to reduce the impacts and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ many studies focus on the threats to cities from sea-level rise or damage to health and water resources , but that these impact estimates do n't take into consideration the " urban heat island " effect . <p> " Any hard-won victories over climate change on a global scale could be wiped out by the effects of uncontrolled urban heat islands , " said Professor Richard SJ Tol , professor of economics at the University of Sussex , UK , in a statement . " We show that city-level adaptation strategies to limit local warming have important economic net benefits for almost all cities around the world . " <p> According to the study , cities cover just 1 percent of the Earth 's surface but house over half of the world 's population , consuming 78 percent of the world 's energy and producing 80 percent of the Gross World Product ( GWP ) , so measures that could limit the impact of rising temperatures should be pretty high priority . <p> They modeled different solutions , including ideas as simple as installing heat-reflective pavements and roofs . They @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ roofs and pavements could reduce temperatures by 0.8 ? C and save up to 12 times what they cost to install and maintain . <p> The worst-case scenario they modeled saw cities such as Tokyo , New York , London , and Beijing lose 10.9 percent of their GDP due to increased spending on the rising costs of energy to keep citizens cool and the price of keeping pollution down . <p> While the world waits for Trump to come to a decision on the Paris climate agreement , perhaps the effects of climate change in terms of economic loss is a language he can understand and a more effective way to reach him and get the message across .

@@18717824 <h> Improving parental leave for council and trustees <p> Municipalities and school boards will be required to have a policy on pregnancy and parental leave for council members and school board trustees . The offices of members of council would not become vacant because of an absence related to pregnancy or parental leave for 20 consecutive weeks or less . Until now , only some municipalities have formal or informal policies regarding pregnancy or parental leave for members that include allowing absences from council meetings . Municipalities could still decide to excuse absences from meetings for any reason , including to provide for pregnancy or parental leave beyond 20 weeks . <h> Broadening municipal investment powers <p> Municipalities will have access to more resources to meet their community 's needs . The changes promote municipal financial flexibility by allowing eligible municipalities to expand the ways they can invest money not immediately needed . This may help municipalities raise more revenues for repairs and replacements of local infrastructure . <h> Addressing climate change <p> Changes to the Municipal Act and the City of Toronto Act better position municipalities to become leaders @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Municipalities will be required to have tree canopy policies , which they can tailor to suit local needs . Municipalities will also be able to require green construction standards in certain situations . This could include giving municipalities the power to require green roofs on new construction . <h> Improving access to justice <p> Municipalities will need to provide access to an integrity commissioner . It would be up to a municipality to decide whether or not to appoint their own full-time integrity commissioner , share the position with other municipalities , or retain someone on a fee-for-services basis . <p> Local integrity commissioners will have a broader role . They will give advice to members of council , as well as provide educational information to the public , the municipality , members of council and some local boards . <p> These changes , along with many other changes in the bill , would come into force on proclamation . <h> Accountability in local government <p> Every municipality in Ontario will need to have a local code of conduct in place for its council members and members of some local @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ conduct of those members and will help ensure that local governments continue to be open and accountable to the communities they serve . <h> Regional council representation <p> To help ensure local representation keeps up with Ontario 's changing demographics , the make-up of regional councils will be regularly considered . Regional municipalities will undertake a mandatory review of regional council composition following every second municipal election . This will allow municipalities to make sure their councils best suit local needs . <h> Additional details <p> Among other matters , the Modernizing Ontario 's Municipal Legislation Act also clarifies the definition of a meeting of municipal council , certain locals boards and committees for specific purposes , removes a limit on municipal by-law powers respecting advertising devices ( such as signs ) , and gives municipalities more tools to establish community hubs.

@@18720987 <h> Stratford Festival marks the sesquicentennial in its 2017 season <p> The 150th anniversary of Canada 's Confederation served as a kind of catalyst for the 2017 season of the Stratford Festival . <p> Thinking about what it means to be Canadian , Festival artistic director Antoni Cimolino began to consider the concept of identity . Given our country 's convoluted history -- and the mosaic of individual and collective identities that contributed to that history -- Cimolino asked a question that seemed particularly apt for the sesquicentennial year . <p> " What 's in a name ? " <p> From that pointed question came the 2017 season 's overarching theme , an exploration of what it means to " call yourself something . " But for Cimolino , this theme was more than a simple examination of self-hood but a way to investigate the consequential conflicts within ourselves -- the inevitable clash between individual and shared identities . <p> That struggle , Cimolino said , becomes central to many of the season 's productions -- serving as a crux for the tragedy of Romeo and Juliet , for example @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> " For instance , Romeo is a Montague . He can either be Romeo the person , who is in love with Juliet , or he can be a Montague who is fighting with the Capulets , " Cimolino said . " He has to somehow navigate those waters . <p> " Sometimes it 's a light-hearted look at how we identify and the implications of that , like HMS Pinafore , where the guy finds out he 's the son of somebody else and that changes his entire life because , suddenly , he 's of another class and can do things he was n't able to before . That 's all because of his identity and not his person . " <p> Through this exploration of identity , Cimolino also wanted to examine the parallel conflict between self-interest and the greater good , particularly through selected identities . <p> " In other plays , like School for Scandal and Tartuffe , people are deliberately hiding their identities , " the artistic director said . " They 're deliberately trying to misrepresent themselves to be able to take @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is n't always in the service of self-interest , Cimolino noted . In the season-opening Twelfth Night , for example , identity is used in a more healing sense -- a voyage of self-discovery through the assumption of another persona . <p> " I wanted to look at all the different ways that identity impacts our lives -- the way we choose identities -- and then that came around to the idea of being Canadian , " Cimolino said . " Different events in our history have helped form who we are . " <p> This season 's production of The Breathing Hole delves into five centuries of Canadian history , starting with Jacques Cartier 's planting of the French flag near the Gulf of the St. Lawrence and culminating with a near-future glimpse of an Artic warmed by climate change . <p> " It examines the different elements of the Canadian identity -- our connection to the land , the fact that the First Nations were here before European contact , the nature of the European contact ... and then what the future might hold for us . " @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ -- is a more cutting consideration of identity . The play explores themes of race , privilege and colonialism by focusing on the federal government 's decision to block more than 300 Sikh immigrants from Canada on the eve of the First World War . <p> " Most of them ( had ) served as part of the British Army and were given guarantees of residency in any part of the Empire , " Cimolino said , " but they were barred from entering Canada . <p> " This was an interesting moment because these were British soldiers -- they served for the Commonwealth -- but they could n't enter Canada because Canada 's British identity was n't strong enough to overcome their aversion they seemed to have for this non-European group landing . But Canada 's British identity was strong enough that we would send hundreds of thousands of young men to die in Europe for a war that did n't really impact us . <p> " So how do we identify ? Who do we identify with ? Do we identify with being part of the Commonwealth or @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , many of the questions posed by the productions remain relevant , particularly those that involve an unflinching look at who we are . @@18729560 <p> Telecommuting to work can save professionals money and greatly reduce the transportation-related emissions produced by commuting to and from the office every day . <p> Recognizing the threat posed by climate change , many people have resolved to live more eco-friendly lifestyles . Reducing vehicle emissions can have a strong and positive impact on the environment and may even benefit the bottom line . <p> The task of reducing vehicle emissions is not as difficult as it may seem , as there are many steps ordinary citizens can take to cut back on the greenhouse gases their vehicles produce each day . <p> Telecommute to work . <p> Recent research from Global Workplace found that 50 per cent of the workforce holds a job that is compatible with at least partial telework . Although there are cost savings , the financial benefits may pale in comparison to the effects that mass telecommuting can have on the planet . Telecommuters consume considerably less fuel than workers who drive or take mass transportation to work , and over time that can greatly reduce transportationrelated greenhouse gas emissions . <p> Prioritize vehicle @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ cost motorists substantial amounts of money . Something as simple as replacing a clogged air filter can improve gas mileage by as much as 10 per cent . In addition , keeping tires properly inflated can reduce drag and improve fuel economy . <p> Avoid idling . <p> Conventional automotive wisdom once suggested that idling a vehicle for several minutes can effectively warm up its engine . That is not the case anymore . Idling for more than 30 seconds can increase air pollution unnecessarily , waste fuel and money , and cause excessive wear and damage to engine components . Auto manufacturers now recommend vehicles idle for no more than 30 seconds before they begin driving , as modern engines take less time to warm up than engines of yesteryear . <p> Drive less . Perhaps the simplest way to reduce vehicle emissions is to drive less . <h> Comments <h> NOTE : To post a comment you must have an account with at least one of the following services : Disqus , Facebook , Twitter , Google+ You may then login using your account credentials for that service @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ may register a new profile with Disqus by first clicking the " Post as " button and then the link : " Do n't have one ? By that definition , every tax in Canadian history would be considered revenue-neutral . <p> Alberta 's carbon tax takes billions from taxpayers and the government plans to spend that money , at least partially , on corporate welfare to big emitters such as oil companies and green-energy corporations . Its coal use is finally flatlining , it 's investing heavily in both nuclear and wind power , and now it 's now home to the world 's largest floating solar farm . <p> Sungrow Power Supply announced this month that they have finished construction on a 40-megawatt solar power plant , which is sitting on a somewhat appropriate setting . The area was once a coal-mining town , but it 's since been flooded . <p> Found offshore from Huainan , it has been successfully connected to the grid . Thanks to its placement offshore , it does n't take up any " space " , and it uses less energy than most solar farms as the seawater acts as a natural coolant . <p> The construction of the plant is part of China 's efforts to become what some are calling @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ becoming a key component of this , with similarly-sized projects cropping up all over China . <p> A venture between privately-owned and state-owned Chinese companies is even converting much of Ukraine 's Chernobyl into a solar power plant . Ly Jinrong/Shutterstock <p> Thanks to market forces turning against fossil fuels , the increasing affordability , and effectiveness of renewable energy , the need to stamp out coal-driven smog outbreaks and the chance to be seen as a benevolent presence on the world stage , China is now moving full steam ahead towards a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of the best ways to achieve this . A recent analysis of the world 's efforts to curb global warming has found that solar farms are the 8th best way to cut GHGs . Solar power is currently responsible for 0.4 percent of the world 's electricity production , but if this grew to 10 percent by 2050 , 39.6 billion tonnes ( 43.7 billion tons ) of carbon dioxide would be prevented from escaping into the atmosphere . <p> In addition , this would result in at least a $5 trillion paycheck for the global economy , through new jobs , less damage from climate change phenomena , and -- primarily -- operational cost savings . <p> Fossil fuels are dirty , increasingly expensive , and harm the planet . China , for all its imperfections , has recognized this , as projects like this floating solar farm clearly show .

@@18737805 <p> John Boyko is the author of eight books addressing Canadian history and politics including Sir John 's Echo . <p> Canada is a conversation . When confronting troubles visited upon us , or of our own making , Canadians reach not for a gun but a gavel . We talk it out . Every leadership race and election , every new bill , public initiative or staggering crisis , and every table pounding in the House of Commons or at the local Tim Hortons is another element of that conversation . And when we 're talking , we 're always talking about power . So , let 's talk . <p> Political power touches us all . Positively expressed , it offers a vehicle through which we are collectively encouraged and enabled to act for the common good . Power matters , and so it matters who has it . <p> Our founders understood . In 1864 , they met in Charlottetown and Quebec City and talked their way into the creation of a country . From Britain came the concepts of a limited monarchy and parliamentary democracy . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a written constitution and a federal state , in Canada 's case one composed of a central government and provinces . This is where the real talking about power began . <p> Sir John A. Macdonald led the way in arguing that while the American Constitution was brilliant in its conception , the fact that the United States was , at that moment , butchering itself in the Civil War demonstrated its appalling failure in practice . Seeing this , the Canadian Confederation delegates decided to stand the American system on its head . Macdonald explained that Canada would reverse the " primary error " of the United States " by strengthening the general government and conferring on the provincial bodies only such powers as may be required for local purposes . " <p> The provinces were given only municipal-like areas of responsibility and a limited ability to raise revenue . The federal government , on the other hand , was afforded the major powers relating to sovereignty , including trade , the military , the post office , criminal law , currency and banking . Unlike in the United @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ senators , in Canada the prime minister was given the power to populate the country 's Senate . The prime minister would also appoint the lieutenant-governors , who approved provincial bills while sending questionable ones to the federal cabinet , which could disallow them . It was decided that responsibility for anything the Constitution left out or that came up later , such as airports , would go automatically to the federal government . <p> Throughout Canada 's 150-year conversation , provinces have worked to overturn our founders ' vision and shift power to themselves . An example is the decades-long provincial demand for greater power that sabotaged repeated federal efforts to earn greater independence for the country by gaining control of our Constitution . In standing up for what they believed was best for their province , too many premiers betrayed and undermined the very concept of Canada while dividing Canadians against themselves . <p> This is not to say that premiers are not patriots and provinces do n't matter . Of course they are and of course they do . But it was successive federal governments that fought @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and dragged along as the federal government led the building of Canada through projects such as the transcontinental railway , St. Lawrence Seaway and the Trans-Canada Highway . The federal government needled , nudged and negotiated for Canadians in creating national policies such as pensions and health care . Federal governments rallied our response to emergencies such as global wars , the Great Depression and the FLQ crisis . The federal government spoke for Canadian values whether reflected as peacekeepers or climate-change leaders . <p> Ignore whether you like or dislike our current Prime Minister or his policies , but grant that his Canadian tour a few months ago indicated his understanding that this country is indeed a conversation . He is also demonstrating that he is the personification of Sir John 's vision . He gathered the premiers and then led the revamping of pensions , unemployment insurance and health care . He told the provinces that we will combat climate change as a country and that they will step in line . His government organized a national emergency response to the Fort McMurray wildfires . <p> We have @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ afforded the federal government was effectively employed . We have gone off the rails when firewall letters , referendums and power squabbles have attempted to distort that vision . We are better when we consider ourselves not as of a particular province but , more broadly , as Canadians first , stronger in the complexity of our citizenship . <p> Every time you hear our Prime Minister speak , listen carefully for a hint of a Scottish burr , for you 're hearing Sir John 's echo . <h> Next story <h> Learn More <h> Discover content from The Globe and Mail that you might otherwise not have come across . In 2018 , the parties to the agreement will undertake an initial ' stock take ' to assess the collection of nationally determined contributions that each party has pledged against the broad goals of the agreement .
